In Central America, at least 60 institutions in seven countries hold active zoological, botanical and paleontological collections. However, only ten publishers in four countries are sharing collection data to GBIF (noting no fossil records are currently shared). Costa Rica and Guatemala have contributed 96 per cent of the available specimen records on GBIF from the region, but three countries, including El Salvador, have not yet mobilized collections to GBIF. Following the priorities established in the 2026 BID Latin America and the Caribbean engagement meeting and Targets 20-21 outlined in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, this project strengthens the collaboration between institutions in Central America by facilitating mentorship from experienced participants to build and sustain regional capacity for collection data mobilization and use (integrating FAIR and CARE principles). This is achieved through expanding the GBIF network in the region. Based on the successful model designed for the Guatemalan collections (comprised of four GBIF publishers, more than 25 collections, 50,000 occurrences and 18,000 images), a customized Symbiota portal will be activated to enable and sustain digitization, management and mobilization of Central American collections to GBIF. During the first year of the project, a series of tailored webinars and open sessions will be facilitated to mobilize 25 new collections (targeting Guatemala, El Salvador and Costa Rica), and review of quality data for more than 40 existing collection datasets. A hybrid meeting in Costa Rica aims to allow partners to interact, share preliminary results and participate in data use training for research and policy making, including validation of 33 checklist datasets. collections"},"body":{"en-GB":"Nigeria’s rich biodiversity collections include herbaria, zoological, entomological, fossils and microbial repositories and support research, conservation planning and sustainable development. However, a large portion of these collections remain inaccessible to global audiences due to low digitization and data sharing. Nigeria has hundreds of biodiversity data holding institutions which have being active since the colonial era that house an array of rich datasets that span over several decades. These invaluable resources are held in cabinets and shelves of herbaria and museums, currently only useful locally as teaching aids or reference materials for identification. It has been reported that 70 per cent of herbaria in Nigeria are globally not indexed and 90 per cent of such collections are not digitized. This project aims to mobilize, clean and digitize specimen data from selected Nigerian biodiversity collections to global biodiversity databases including GBIF. National commitments under Targets two (restoration), nine (sustainable use) and 10 (forest biodiversity) depend on accessible, interoperable occurrence data, yet large volumes of plant records from Southern Africa (e.g. Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, and South Africa) remain unpublished or stored in non-standardized formats. This project aims to collect, digitize and standardize occurrence records for trees and shrubs plants across woodland landscapes, publishing them as open-access datasets through GBIF. These needs were identified through analysis of GBIF data coverage, consultations within the SEOSAW (Socio-Ecological Observatory for Studying African Woodlands) network and national biodiversity assessments highlighting critical taxonomic and geographic gaps. The project builds on prior [BID support](/project/d5AD8O2jAcecQIGawemcI/mobilization-of-data-on-non-timber-forest-species-in-biodiversity-hotspots-of-zimbabwe), which developed capacity in data mobilization, Darwin Core standardization and stakeholder engagement.
